channel.title: Bottleneck by Jun Wei
channel.description: Explainers on the companies and industries the world can't do without.

item.title: An ETF for Every Theory: The Strangest Funds
item.description: ETFs began as a cheap way to own the whole market. Now there's one for almost any idea: copying Congress, backing a party, betting against a fund manager or a TV stock-picker, or trading fear itself. What's inside them, and the boring fund they're all up against.

item.title: What's a Bond Worth? How Bond Prices and Yields Work
item.description: A bond is a promise to pay fixed amounts on fixed dates. Working out what that promise is worth today explains why prices fall when rates rise, why a risk-free Treasury can lose you money, why a 9% corporate bond may not return 9%, and why some bonds swing far more than others.

item.title: Ask Why: The Rise and Fall of Enron
item.description: For six years running, Fortune named Enron America's most innovative company. In 2001 it went bankrupt and took its auditor down with it. How a pipeline company turned into a trading house, booked profits it hadn't earned, hid losses in its finance chief's partnerships, and fell apart when people finally asked.

item.title: The Debt That Nearly Broke the Euro: Greece's Crisis
item.description: In 2001 Greece squeezed into the euro. Eight years later a new government admitted the budget figures had been wrong. How Greece got in, what it hid, why three bailouts and years of austerity left its debt higher than before, and what the crisis says about sharing a currency.

item.title: The Rumour That Emptied a Bank: How Bank Runs Work
item.description: In December 1973 a schoolgirl's joke on a Japanese train sent thousands of people to queue outside a healthy bank. How banks lend out most of what you deposit, why a cash shortage can turn into a collapse, and the tools governments use to keep the queues away.

item.title: Betting on a Fall: How Short Selling Works
item.description: Most investors make money when prices rise. Short sellers borrow shares, sell them, and hope to buy them back cheaper. They're blamed when markets fall and, now and then, they're the first to spot a fraud. How shorting works, who lends the shares, how to read the numbers, and why a crowded short can blow up.

item.title: The Safety Lab That Became a Juggernaut: The Anthropic Story
item.description: In late 2020 seven researchers walked out of OpenAI. Six years later the company they founded is worth about $1.5 trillion and has fought the Pentagon in court. How Anthropic got there, where the accounts of its rise disagree, and the strongest case its critics make.

item.title: Chu and Han: From the First Emperor’s Death to Empress Lü’s, 210–180 BC
item.description: In 210 BC the First Emperor of Qin died on the road, and his empire outlived him by three years. Then came the war between Xiang Yu and Liu Bang, the purge of the generals who won it, and fifteen years of Empress Lü. A scrolling map, year by year, and one life followed through it: Liu Bang, Lü Zhi, Zhang Liang, Han Xin, Xiang Yu or Fan Zeng.

item.title: Reading the Squiggles: How Traders Read a Price Chart
item.description: Candlesticks, Point and Figure, Kagi and Renko charts, golden and death crosses, RSI, MACD and a dozen other momentum studies: what technical analysts look at, how each tool is built, and what the evidence says about whether any of it works.

item.title: The Dark Wizard: How Hjalmar Schacht Paid for Hitler's Rearmament
item.description: In 1933 six million Germans were out of work. By 1939 unemployment had all but vanished and Hitler was parading a new army, built by a country short of gold, oil and rubber. Much of the financing was engineered by one central banker, Hjalmar Schacht. Here is how the tricks worked, what they hid, and what they cost.

item.title: What Is a Company Worth? Reading P/E, EV and EBITDA
item.description: A share price on its own says almost nothing. Valuation ratios turn a price into a comparison: what you pay for each dollar of sales, profit or cash. Here is what each common ratio measures, when to use which, and where the numbers come from.

item.title: Shrinking the Pie: How Stock Buybacks Work
item.description: When a company buys back its own shares, it isn't placing one giant order. It buys slowly, through a broker, only from people who choose to sell, under rules that cap how much it can buy each day, and it can stop whenever it likes.

item.title: Who Gets the Biggest Slice? How Stock Indexes Weight Companies
item.description: The S&P 500, the Dow and an equal-weight fund can hold the same companies in very different amounts, because each uses a different rule for how much each company counts. Here are the three rules, what they do to your money, and why a stock split can change a company's place in the Dow.

item.title: The Saver's Ladder: From Fixed Deposits to Stocks
item.description: A fixed deposit, a Singapore Savings Bond, a corporate bond, an ETF and a single stock are all places to park the same dollar. Each step up offers more expected return and asks you to accept more ways to lose. Here is what you own on each rung, who promises what, and what 125 years of history say about the climb.

item.title: The $9.6 Trillion Market: How Forex Works
item.description: Every day about $9.6 trillion of currencies changes hands, more than any other market. Most of it is banks and funds you never see; a sliver is people at home trading with borrowed money. Here is who trades forex, how to read a currency pair, why leverage pulls traders in, and what happens when a currency breaks.

item.title: What Happens When You Press Send: Inside an AI Answer
item.description: Every chatbot reply is a short trip through a data centre: tokenised, routed, batched, read in one burst and written one token at a time. Follow one message along that path, see why mixture-of-experts models change the arithmetic, and why Groq and Taalas bet on opposite chips to make it faster.

item.title: The Biggest Bubble in History: Japan's Lost Decades
item.description: By 1989 Japan was the world's second-largest economy, home to 32 of the 50 biggest companies, with land under Tokyo's Imperial Palace said to be worth more than all of California. Then the bubble burst. Here is how post-war Japan rose so fast, how a feedback loop between land and shares inflated the biggest asset bubble in history, and why the fall became two lost decades.

item.title: Three Companies, One Industry: AMD vs Intel vs Nvidia
item.description: Intel once owned the processor. Today the fight splits across different markets: server and PC chips, AI accelerators, gaming graphics and embedded. In each, the leader is different. Here is who holds what, and how it got that way.

item.title: Three Kingdoms: How the Han Empire Broke Apart, 184–280
item.description: In 184 a religious rising shook the Han empire, and the generals who put it down never gave their armies back. For the next century they and their heirs fought over China until three states were left: Wei, Shu and Wu. A scrolling map of the borders, and one life followed through it: Cao Cao, Liu Bei, Sun Quan, Zhuge Liang, Guan Yu or Sima Yi.

item.title: The Domino Year: How the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis Spread
item.description: In July 1997 Thailand ran out of dollars defending its currency and let the baht float. It fell, and the panic jumped from one Asian economy to the next: Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, then South Korea, in months. The IMF arrived with the largest rescues in its history and conditions that still divide economists. Here is how the dominoes fell, and what the bailouts did.

item.title: The Lord's Cut: How Seigniorage Lets Money-Makers Profit
item.description: Make a dollar for a few cents and spend it at face value, and you keep the difference. That gap is seigniorage, the oldest profit in finance. Medieval lords took it by minting coins and quietly shaving the silver out of them. Today a government, a bank and a stablecoin issuer each take a version of it. Here is how the same trick has worked from the mint to the blockchain.

item.title: Hedge or Bet? How Derivatives Work
item.description: A derivative is a contract whose value comes from something else: a price, a rate, an index. Farmers and airlines use them to lock in costs; speculators use them to bet with borrowed size, or to bet that a price will fall. In 2002 Warren Buffett called them "financial weapons of mass destruction." Here is what they are, why they are useful, and how the same tools helped blow up LTCM, AIG and the 2008 crisis.

item.title: Keeping a Coin Worth a Dollar: How Stablecoins Hold (and Lose) Their Peg
item.description: A stablecoin promises to be worth one dollar. Some hold that promise with cash in a bank, some with crypto locked in a contract, and some with nothing but code and confidence. The last kind wiped out about $40 billion in three days. Here's what keeps a dollar a dollar, and what breaks it.

item.title: Lending to Governments: US Treasuries vs Singapore's Bonds
item.description: A bond is a loan you make to a government. The US borrows to spend and now pays more interest than it spends on defence. Singapore borrows more, relative to its economy, yet almost none of it funds spending. Two countries, two very different reasons to issue debt.

item.title: One Seesaw, Two Fears: How the Fed Uses the Bond Market
item.description: The Fed aims for 2% inflation. Afraid of a slump in 2020, it pushed bond prices up and yields down; afraid of inflation in 2022–23, it did the reverse. One price-yield seesaw explains both.

item.title: The Crystal Behind Your Scan and Your Screen: Who Controls the World's Iodine
item.description: Iodine goes into CT-scan dye and the films inside LCD screens. About two-thirds of it comes from one Chilean desert, one company says it sells about 37% of the world's supply, and the price has more than tripled since 2017.

item.title: The Bank Behind the Currency Market: How CLS Keeps FX Trades From Going Wrong
item.description: More than US$14 trillion of currency trades come due every day, in two currencies across two clocks. One little-known New York bank, CLS, locks the two halves together for 18 currencies, Singapore's among them. Yet only about a third of the market settles that safely.

item.title: The Price Behind the Price: Who Sets the Number Oil Is Sold Against
item.description: Most of the world's exported crude oil is sold against a number that a news-and-data firm fixes once a day, from a thin slice of trades. One of those numbers, Dubai, has less and less Dubai in it. This month, Abu Dhabi moved its own crude onto it.

item.title: The Insurer Nobody Sees: Twelve Clubs Behind Every Big Ship
item.description: Whenever a big ship hits something, a bill lands on a company you have almost certainly never heard of. Twelve mutual clubs insure about 90% of the world's ocean-going tonnage and share one tower of cover. In 2024 a Singapore-flagged ship pushed it to its last layer.

item.title: From a $2 Stock to the Trillion-Dollar Club: How AMD Came Back
item.description: In July 2015 AMD closed at $1.62 and analysts wondered if it would survive. Under Lisa Su it passed Intel, won OpenAI as an AI-chip customer, and briefly topped $1 trillion in September 2026.
